title: Detecting Interference in Online Controlled Experiments with Increasing Allocation

problem.claim: Interference among units in settings such as social networks and bipartite online marketplaces can harm the validity of simple inference procedures for A/B tests with increasing treatment allocation.

gap.claim: A procedure is needed to test for interference in A/B testing with increasing allocation without requiring a specific interference mechanism in advance.

contributions.claim: The work introduces a widely applicable procedure for testing interference in A/B testing with increasing allocation.
The work introduces two permutation tests valid under different assumptions: a general test requiring no additional assumption and a test valid under a time fixed effect assumption.
The procedure can be implemented on an existing A/B testing platform through a separate flow without requiring an a priori specific interference mechanism.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the testing procedure has very low computational complexity and is powerful.
The authors report demonstrating the performance of the proposed testing procedure through simulations on synthetic data.
The authors discuss an application at LinkedIn in which a screening step uses the proposed methods to detect potential interference in marketplace experiments.

narrative_sequence.summary: Online controlled experiments are widely used to guide business decisions, and treatment allocation is often increased gradually through a sequence of randomized experiments.
Interference among units can undermine simple inference procedures in social-network and bipartite-marketplace experiments.
The work proposes a platform-compatible procedure and two permutation tests for detecting interference under different assumptions.
The authors report low computational complexity, power, and formalization of an industry heuristic.
The authors report synthetic-data simulations and discuss a LinkedIn screening application for marketplace experiments.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the test statistics, assumptions in detail, or implementation procedure.
The abstract does not report simulation configurations, quantitative results, or comparisons.
The abstract does not provide quantitative details about the LinkedIn application.
